messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Gerald is a 62-year-old potter, married, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 60 following the sudden and traumatic death of a loved one. He was referred for psychological assessment after his wife expressed concern about changes in his personality and functioning over the preceding months. Gerald arrived at the intake appointment quietly dressed, speaking in measured tones, his hands — accustomed to shaping clay — resting still in his lap in a way that seemed unfamiliar even to him.

The loss came without warning. Gerald had not had the chance to prepare, to say what needed saying, or to move through any of the ordinary rituals of anticipatory grief. The death arrived as a rupture, and in its aftermath Gerald found that the world continued turning in a way that felt obscene. Friends sent food. His wife tried to talk. The studio, where he had spent thirty years with his hands in wet earth, remained as it had always been — and that, somehow, was the worst of it. The smell of the clay, the particular grey light through the workshop windows on a winter morning, the sound of the wheel — all of it had once been saturated with a shared life, with conversations and visits and the easy presence of someone who was now gone. To return to work was to walk directly into that absence.

What Gerald developed in the months that followed was a set of strategies that felt, to him, not like avoidance but like survival. He had come to believe, in a way he could not fully articulate but felt with absolute conviction, that positive emotion was dangerous — that to feel pleasure or warmth or even ordinary contentment was to betray the dead, or worse, to lower his guard against a world that had already shown it could take everything without notice. When his wife laughed at something on television and he felt the reflex of his own smile begin, he pressed it down. He described this in session not as a choice but as a reflex of protection, a sealing off. Joy, in his current understanding of the world, was simply the leading edge of future devastation.

His avoidance of grief reminders had reshaped his daily life in ways that were increasingly difficult to conceal. Gerald had stopped entering the room in his home where certain photographs were kept. He had rerouted his morning walk to avoid passing a particular café. Most significantly, he had found himself unable to work with a specific line of ceramic pieces — vessels he had been developing for years — because the design had been shaped in conversation with the person he lost. The studio, once the center of his identity and livelihood, had become a place he entered only when necessary, moving through it with a kind of deliberate blankness, avoiding the corner where those unfinished pieces still sat under their cloth. A commission he had accepted months before the death remained incomplete, and a gallery relationship he had cultivated for years was quietly fraying.

Perhaps most telling was Gerald's complete withdrawal from any thought of the future. He had stopped making plans — not in the dramatic sense, but in the small, accumulative sense that constitutes a life. He no longer booked ahead for anything. He had declined an invitation to a residency he would previously have welcomed. When his wife mentioned a trip they had discussed for years, he changed the subject. He had come to feel that planning was a form of presumption — that to imagine a future was to invite the same kind of sudden erasure that had already found him once. The future, in his mind, was simply where loss lived.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was his wife's quiet statement, one evening, that she felt she had lost him too. He had not cried when she said it. But he had made the appointment the following morning. What he most fears is that the person he was before the loss is also gone. What he most hopes, though he would not use this word, is that it might be possible to return to the wheel.
